item.title: The world’s richest people have discovered a new way to give their money away: a couple hundred bucks to one kid at a time.
item.content:encoded: Since John D. Rockefeller handed out dimes, the world’s richest have given away their money in very different ways. Now they are bypassing charity—and writing a new social contract.

item.title: Canada Retail Sales Look to Build on August’s Rebound
item.content:encoded: Retail spending by Canadians looks to have remained on the rise last month, though the pace is showing signs of cooling as uncertainty and gasoline prices remain high.

item.title: Consumer Sentiment Declined Slightly in October
item.content:encoded: The University of Michigan survey’s headline index came in at 48, down from 48.1 in September and hovering near record-low levels.

item.title: American Express is slashing around 3,500 jobs globally in an attempt to put a cap on rising costs
item.content:encoded: The credit-card company is the latest to announce job cuts this week as Barclays, eBay and Volvo also lay off thousands of employees.

item.title: Economic damage from high energy prices and rising borrowing costs is mounting globally, splitting the world into a new set of winners and losers as countries with limited exposure to the AI boom fall behind
item.content:encoded: The fallout from higher energy and borrowing costs is deepening across the world, hitting harder for countries with limited exposure to the technology.

item.title: U.S. Housing Starts Dropped Again in September
item.content:encoded: Housing starts fell 5.2% in September to 1.221 million. Economists had expected a reading of 1.3 million and for starts to rise 2% over the month.

item.title: Canada Building Permits Rebound in August
item.content:encoded: The total value of building permits rose 8.8% from the month before to a seasonally adjusted 13.57 billion Canadian dollars, the equivalent of $9.55 billion, Statistics Canada said.

item.title: Philippines Central Bank Surprises With Big Rate Hike to Combat Inflation
item.content:encoded: The Philippine central bank raised interest rates by more than expected Thursday, warning that inflation would accelerate further as renewed Middle East tensions pushed up energy prices.

item.title: Consumer Sentiment Ticked Lower in September
item.content:encoded: The University of Michigan survey’s headline index landed at 48.1 in September, down from 51.7 in August.

item.title: Capital Account: President Trump once called “tariff” the most beautiful word in the dictionary. He has somehow made it one of the most hated words in politics, writes @greg_ip
item.content:encoded: President Trump’s tariffs collided with public anxiety over the cost of living. Now his trade legacy is at risk.

item.title: French Contraction Has Slowed Eurozone Expansion, Surveys Show
item.content:encoded: Business activity in the eurozone slowed in October amid a squeeze on profit margins, a sign of fading resilience in the face of the higher energy costs.

item.title: IMF Warns Governments Against Reliance on Short-Term Debt
item.content:encoded: The IMF warned that as inflation shocks become frequent, governments’ shift to selling more short-term debt may have the opposite effect to the one intended.

item.title: U.S. Home-Builder Sentiment Sinks to 14-Year Low
item.content:encoded: The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index, a gauge of builder confidence in the market for newly built single family housing, fell three points to 29 in October. That’s the lowest reading since June 2012.

item.title: America’s home-buying market is a house divided as surging mortgage rates send many buyers to the sidelines, while the affluent drive overall prices higher with big cash purchases
item.content:encoded: Surging mortgage rates are sending many buyers to the sidelines, while affluent shoppers are driving overall prices higher with big cash purchases.

item.title: Canada Housing Starts Rise in September, Though Market Faces Longer-Term Supply Gap
item.content:encoded: Canadian housing starts picked up last month though the pace remains soft as the broader market shows signs of cooling into the end of the year.

item.title: Eurozone Consumer Inflation Expectations Edged Higher in September
item.content:encoded: Consumers expected prices to rise more than they did in August, as energy prices continued to rise as the war in the Middle East dragged on.

item.title: Bank of Korea Holds Rate Steady After Back-to-Back Hikes
item.content:encoded: South Korea’s central bank held its policy rate steady as expected after two consecutive increases, pausing its tightening as inflation eased but remained above target.

item.title: Consumer Sentiment Drops, per Michigan Survey
item.content:encoded: The University of Michigan survey’s headline index fell to 46.3 in its preliminary October reading, versus 48.1 in September.

item.title: U.S. consumer spending is on the rise despite frustrations with persistent inflation and gloomy views about the economy
item.content:encoded: Spending is rising because prices are climbing and Americans are buying more stuff.

item.title: Lutnick Throws the Future of U.S.-Mexico Trade Talks Into Further Doubt
item.content:encoded: The commerce secretary has objected to significant reductions in tariffs on Mexican steel, aluminum and automobiles.
